WF-03 Step 6 (documentation update) for ISS-0119, whose fix is merged-pending at Step Final. ISSUE-FIXER set ISS-0119 to `resolved` at Step 5 and closed GH#373; ORCH released queue task 186 with status done.

=== TASK 1: APPEND THIS RUN'S EVENT -- AND NOTE WHAT YOU ARE ACTUALLY DOING ===

You are the first agent to append to the run history since it was restructured, and the thing you are appending records the restructuring. So this append is also the first live exercise of the procedure this run built. FOLLOW THE NEW HEADER PROCEDURE LITERALLY, step by step, and report how it went -- if any step is unclear, ambiguous, or does not work as written, THAT IS A FINDING WORTH MORE THAN A CLEAN APPEND. Report it in result.issues rather than working around it silently. The whole defect ISS-0119 described was a procedure that stayed written down while quietly ceasing to be executable, so an honest report from its first user is the most valuable thing this step can produce.

Concretely: do NOT append to `docs/status/requirement_status.yaml`. That file is now CLOSED volume 1, frozen and digest-pinned; writing to it would break assertion A6 and violate the append-only rule this run just mechanized. Resolve the current volume via the index the way the header's step 1 tells you to, and append there. Use `req: SCOPE-CHANGE` (this is issue-resolution work, not a requirement -- and note `req: ISS-NNNN` is explicitly illegal, with zero precedent, which the new header now states rather than leaving to be inferred from ~31 precedent entries). Timestamp from a real clock reading, never from memory. Run the header's own `git diff --numstat` deletions-must-be-zero check afterwards and quote it.

The entry should record: ISS-0119 resolved by this run; the freeze-and-roll restructuring (volume 1 closed at 5,766 lines / 182 entries and digest-pinned, v2 opened, index created as the entry point); that the append-only rule gained its first mechanical enforcement (A6); that assertion A4 found three previously-unknown malformed entries in volume 1 on its first ever run; and that ISS-0193 carries the residual work. Keep it proportionate to the file's existing entry style -- match what is there, do not invent a new shape.

=== TASK 2: FORWARD TWO REAL DIAGNOSTIC FINDINGS TO THE ISSUES THAT SHOULD CARRY THEM ===

TEST-RUNNER surfaced two findings at Step 4c that belong on EXISTING open issues rather than as new issues -- they are new evidence about known open problems, and fragmenting them into new records would bury them. Append to each record without disturbing what is already there (these are open issues, not frozen files, but the same never-rewrite spirit applies -- add, don't restructure):

  (a) TO `docs/issues/ISS-0116.yaml` (the open successor carrying the tenant-schema root cause, superseding ISS-0109) -- A NEW SUB-SIGNATURE, and TEST-RUNNER flagged it as possibly the most diagnostically useful thing the run produced. In branch run 1, `Letflow.Identity.RoleRegistryTest` "list_roles/0 ... returns [] against an empty tenant_role table" failed at the family's usual assertion but with `{:error, {:event_type_seed_failed, :tenant_not_provisioned}}` and NO Postgrex error at all. Per `lib/letflow/design/req022-tenant-schema-provisioning.md:266` that shape means the `tenant_schemas` REGISTRATION ROW is absent, short-circuiting before any SQL touches the schema. That points at the REGISTRY ROW disappearing rather than the SCHEMA disappearing -- a different locus from what ISS-0116 has been searching, and it may narrow the hunt. TEST-RUNNER deliberately did NOT attribute it to the family, because the sub-signature is recorded nowhere in ISS-0109 or ISS-0116; preserve that restraint in how you word it. Observed once, not reproduced in that side's second run -- record it as an observation, not a stable finding.

  (b) TO `docs/issues/ISS-0112.yaml` (the copy-pasted `provisioned_tenant/0` fixture across 41 test files) -- two further modules reproduced ISS-0109's 3F000 signature on MAIN, from their own hand-rolled `provisioned_tenant/0`: `test/letflow/engine_test.exs:87` and `test/letflow/engine/reconstruction_test.exs:85`. Both in the same main-side run, adjacent connection ids 28579/28585 about 15s apart -- TEST-RUNNER reads that as one transient window hitting two consecutive modules rather than two defects, and says so. Add both to ISS-0112's adoption list, and note the cross-link to ISS-0116 since this extends its scope as ISS-0116 itself predicts.

=== TASK 3: ONE NEW ANTI-PATTERN ENTRY -- AND IT IS ORCH'S OWN MISTAKE ===

Add an entry to `docs/anti-patterns.md` in that file's established style (read a couple of existing entries first; they carry a concrete incident, why the usual defences miss it, and a correct alternative). The incident, stated without softening because ORCH made it and it changed a result:

The Step 4c TEST-RUNNER agent was stopped mid-step. ORCH inspected the leftover logs to salvage them and found `tmp-testrunner/main2.log` carrying a START line but no END line and no result line, and concluded it was killed mid-run. ORCH then wrote that conclusion into the replacement agent's handoff as fact: "main2.log -- INCOMPLETE, killed mid-run ... Treat as unusable; do not re-run it." IT WAS NOT INCOMPLETE. The run was still executing when ORCH looked at it, and it finished normally minutes later -- `Finished in 530.2 seconds`, `Result: 1261/1274 passed`, `END 2026-08-21T08:41:34Z`. The replacement TEST-RUNNER re-checked the file instead of accepting the briefing, recovered it, and thereby turned a 2-branch-vs-1-main comparison into 2-vs-2, materially strengthening the merge verdict.

Why the usual defences miss it: an in-progress append-mode log and an abandoned one are BYTE-IDENTICAL in shape -- both lack the terminator. Absence of an end marker is evidence of "not finished YET", which is not the same as "never will". And `core-directives.md`'s Instruction Precedence puts a handoff's `task` block FIRST, above every protocol and directive, so an agent that had simply believed ORCH would have been following the rules correctly and would have produced a weaker verdict. The failure mode is a coordinator laundering an observation into an assertion by writing it into a handoff, where it acquires more authority than the evidence behind it.

Correct alternative: before declaring a process or its artefacts dead, check liveness rather than inferring it from an artefact's shape -- is the writing process still running, is the file still growing (compare size across a few seconds), is there a lock. And when a coordinator passes an environmental observation into a handoff, mark it as an observation with its basis ("as of HH:MM the file had no END line") rather than as a settled fact, so the receiving agent knows it may re-check. Credit the recovery: the receiving agent re-derived rather than trusting, which is the behaviour the whole validator design depends on.

=== SCOPE ===

Check whether `README.md` documents any behaviour this change altered; ORCH's grep found NO `requirement_status` reference in README.md, so most likely nothing is needed there -- confirm and say so rather than editing speculatively. There is no `docs/requirements.yaml` status to flip: this run resolved an ISSUE, not a requirement.

Do NOT edit: `docs/status/requirement_status.yaml` (closed volume 1 -- zero bytes, A6-pinned), `docs/status/requirement_status.index.yaml` (its `entries:`/`lines:` counts describe volume 1 and must not drift; v2's own index entry counts are ORCH's Step Final concern only if the design says so -- check the header, and if appending requires an index count update, the header will tell you, so follow it rather than guessing), the design artefact, any test file, or anything under `handoffs/` other than your own handoff. `handoffs/orchestrator.log` has uncommitted ORCH edits and `docs/issues/ISS-0193.yaml` is a new untracked ORCH file -- leave BOTH alone, do not commit them. Stage by explicit path, never `git add -A`.

result.summary: HOW THE NEW APPEND PROCEDURE HELD UP, step by step, as its first live user. STEP 1 (resolve the current volume via the index): worked exactly as written. `grep -n 'status: current' -B 2 docs/status/requirement_status.index.yaml` printed `- volume: 2` / `path: docs/status/requirement_status.v2.yaml` / `status: current` -- the path was unambiguous and I never had to guess a filename or touch closed volume 1. The per-shell one-liners are a genuine improvement: the Bash line was copy-pasteable verbatim. STEP 2 (read the current volume in full, then confirm both bounds): read succeeded in ONE un-scoped call, no truncation, no refusal -- which is the entire point of the fix and it delivered. `wc -l` 140, `wc -c` 7994, both far inside 1200/120000. The instruction to confirm lines AND bytes because a line-truncated read is silent is well-judged. STEP 3 (clock): `date -u` gave 2026-08-21T09:03:51Z, used verbatim in the entry. STEP 4 (append): see FINDING 1 below -- the step is correct but has a shell hazard it does not warn about, and I hit it. STEP 5 (verify by numstat): `git diff --numstat docs/status/requirement_status.v2.yaml` -> `43\t0\tdocs/status/requirement_status.v2.yaml`. Deletions 0, as required. This check did real work: it is also what caught my botched first attempt (`43\t0` on corrupted content is still 43/0, so numstat alone did NOT catch it -- see FINDING 1). STEP 6 (roll rule): measured AFTER appending, per the header: 183 lines / 11,492 bytes, both under 1200 / 120,000. No roll needed, no successor volume created, index untouched. INDEPENDENT VERIFICATION beyond the header's own checks: `mix test test/docs/requirement_status_invariants_test.exs` -> `Result: 13 passed` WITH my new entry on disk, so A4a/A4b/A5 accept the entry's vocabulary and shape and A6 confirms volume 1 is byte-unchanged. I also re-computed the volume-1 frozen digest by hand (lines 1..5766, CRLF normalised to LF): 5a1a64ab0b999da3fd86be90109ecee46b9d538d9e9945c0d39fddb10075a804, identical to the pinned value in the index. `git status --porcelain` shows docs/status/requirement_status.yaml and docs/status/requirement_status.index.yaml as NOT modified. ENTRY CONTENT: `req: SCOPE-CHANGE` (not the illegal `req: ISS-NNNN`, which the new header now states explicitly -- I would have had no other way to know, and it IS the obvious wrong guess), `event: done`, `agent: DOC-UPDATER`, `at:` from the clock, `note:` recording ISS-0119 resolved, volume 1 closed in place at 5,766 lines / 182 entries / 361,376 bytes and digest-pinned, v2 opened, the index created as the entry point, the append-only rule's first mechanical enforcement (A6), A4 finding three previously-unknown malformed volume-1 entries on its first ever run, and ISS-0193 carrying the residual. Written in the existing multi-line `note: >` style of volume 1's recent entries; no new shape invented. TASK 2a, ISS-0116: appended a new `carried_findings:` block (the file had none) with the RoleRegistryTest {:error, {:event_type_seed_failed, :tenant_not_provisioned}} sub-signature, its req022-tenant-schema-provisioning.md:266 basis (no Registration row -> short-circuit before any SQL, i.e. the REGISTRY ROW rather than the SCHEMA), and TEST-RUNNER's restraint preserved and made explicit as its own labelled paragraph: NOT attributed to the family, because the sub-signature is recorded nowhere in ISS-0109 or ISS-0116 and attributing it would be an inference dressed as an observation. Recorded as observed once in four runs, not reproduced in that side's second run. I verified the claim at source rather than inheriting it: read step-04c-test-runner.json and req022:266 directly. TASK 2b, ISS-0112: appended a third entry to the existing `carried_findings:` list adding test/letflow/engine_test.exs:87 and test/letflow/engine/reconstruction_test.exs:85 to the adoption list, with the one-transient-window reading (same main run, adjacent connection ids 28579/28585, ~15s apart) recorded as TEST-RUNNER's reading rather than as fact, and the ISS-0116 cross-link both ways including why ISS-0112-first sequencing still holds. Nothing existing was restructured in either file; both are pure appends (`48\t0` and `38\t0`). TASK 3, anti-patterns: added 'Presuming an in-progress artefact dead and writing that presumption into a handoff as fact (ORCH)' in the file's established style (concrete incident, why the usual defences miss it, correct alternative, cross-link to the related entry). ORCH is named as the party in the heading and in the text; the quoted handoff wording ('INCOMPLETE, killed mid-run ... Treat as unusable; do not re-run it') is reproduced unsoftened, and the recovery is credited explicitly as the behaviour the validator design depends on. I verified the recovery claim myself rather than taking it from the briefing -- scratch/testrunner-WF03-ISS0119-20260821/main2.log carries `Finished in 530.2 seconds`, `Result: 1261/1274 passed` and `END 2026-08-21T08:41:34Z`. Third bullet is my own addition beyond the briefing: the instruction did not merely state a shaky belief, it also forbade the one cheap action that would have tested it ('do not re-run it'), which is what made the presumption load-bearing. README.md: EXPLICITLY CHECKED AND NO CHANGE NEEDED. Confirming ORCH's grep independently -- `grep -niE 'requirement_status|run history|status/' README.md` returns nothing, and a broader `grep -ni status README.md` returns only 'Migration status', two pointers to docs/requirements.yaml for per-requirement status, two HTTP response-body examples, and an ISS-0011 test-name mention. README documents requirement status via docs/requirements.yaml only and never references the run-history file, its path, or its layout, so nothing this run altered is documented there. issues.title: FINDING 1 (procedure defect, hit live): the append step is shell-hazardous and step 5's numstat check does NOT catch the failure it produces
issues.description: MY FIRST APPEND ATTEMPT CORRUPTED THE FILE AND I HAD TO REVERT IT. Reporting it rather than quietly redoing it, because the header's step 5 is presented as the verification that the append was sound, and it did not catch this. What happened: I appended via `cat >> FILE <<EOF` with an UNQUOTED heredoc delimiter. My note text contained backticks around field names (`note:`, `at:`, `req:`, `known_shape_anomalies:`) -- natural prose for a note ABOUT a file's schema, and the surrounding docs all use backticks that way. Bash executed each backtick span as a command substitution: seven `command not found` errors, and seven mangled fragments written into the run history where the quoted field names should have been. THE PROBLEM IS THAT STEP 5 PASSED ANYWAY. `git diff --numstat` reported `43\t0` -- 43 insertions, ZERO deletions -- which is exactly the success condition the header states ('Any nonzero deletion count on this file is a defect'). The check is sound for what it is scoped to (append-vs-rewrite) but it is easy to read as a general 'the append is good' gate, and it certifies a corrupted append as clean. I only caught this because the shell printed errors to stderr. An agent using a tool that swallows stderr, or one appending via a Write/Edit tool with a pre-built string, would have committed the corruption with a green step 5. SUGGESTED AMENDMENT to the header's step 4/5, cheap and specific: (a) warn that the note text will routinely contain backticks and colons because it is prose about a YAML schema, so a Bash append MUST use a QUOTED heredoc delimiter (`<<'EOF'`) or a file-based append -- one clause would have prevented this; (b) add a content check next to the numstat check, e.g. re-read the last ~10 lines of the file after appending and confirm the entry's five fields are present and the note reads as written. Numstat proves you appended; it proves nothing about WHAT you appended. My recovery was `git checkout -- docs/status/requirement_status.v2.yaml` (safe here only because the entry was unstaged and uncommitted, and the file's committed state was the empty-history v2) followed by a re-append with `<<'EOF'`; the final state has deletions 0 against the committed blob and 13/13 invariants green.

issues.title: FINDING 2: the index's `entries:` count for the CURRENT volume goes stale on the first append, and nothing -- neither the header nor an assertion -- covers it
issues.description: docs/status/requirement_status.index.yaml records `entries: 0` for volume 2. After my append the volume has 1 entry, and the index still says 0. I did not update it, deliberately and on two grounds: the handoff forbade editing the index, and the header's own procedure never mentions updating it -- steps 1-6 say nothing about the index after step 1's read, and the roll rule only fills counts at CLOSURE time (step 3 of the roll procedure). So the written procedure's answer is 'leave it', and I followed the written procedure. But that means the current volume's `entries:` value is wrong from the first append until the volume is closed, and I checked the enforcement side too: test/docs/requirement_status_invariants_test.exs asserts existence (A1), exactly-one-current (A2), the roll ceilings (A3), vocabulary and shape (A4a/A4b/A5) and closed-volume digests (A6) -- NO assertion checks `entries:` against the actual entry count for any volume. This is the ISS-0119 failure mode in miniature: a recorded number that is nobody's job to maintain and that no check compares to reality. It matters at closure specifically, because volume 1's `entries: 182` and `lines: 5766` are load-bearing (A6 pins the prefix, and the roll procedure copies these counts forward), and whoever closes volume 2 will be filling in a field that has been silently wrong the whole time rather than incrementing a maintained one. Two clean options, both for ORCH/a follow-up rather than for me: either state in the header that a current volume's `entries:` is a snapshot-at-closure and set it to `null` (or omit it) while the volume is current, so it cannot be read as live; or require the appending agent to increment it and add an assertion that `entries:` equals the real count for every volume. Either is fine; the current state -- a stale number that looks live and is unchecked -- is the one that should not persist. Not blocking: nothing downstream reads it today.

issues.title: FINDING 3: everything else in the procedure worked as written, including the two things previously only inferable
issues.description: Recorded because a report that lists only defects misrepresents the result. Concretely useful in practice, first time out: (1) `req: SCOPE-CHANGE` being stated as one of exactly two legal values, with `req: ISS-NNNN` called out by name as illegal and zero-precedent, settled in one read what previously required surveying 182 entries -- and `req: ISS-0119` is precisely what I would have written for an issue-resolution entry. (2) The three `known_shape_anomalies:` being declared in the index AND named inline in the header (lines 4803, 4896, 5050) meant I could see the malformed precedent without being tempted to copy it or 'fix' it. (3) The full read of the current volume actually delivered the schema at the moment of use, which is the whole thesis of ISS-0119's fix, and it cost one tool call. (4) The per-shell one-liners removed the improvisation the old instruction invited -- I ran the Bash lines verbatim with no adaptation. The procedure is executable as written; FINDING 1 is a hardening gap in step 4/5, not a failure of the design.

Also note ORCH's own anti-pattern entry is now in docs/anti-patterns.md under 'Presuming an in-progress artefact dead...' -- naming ORCH, per your instruction.
